strings.title: Adding Near a Ten
strings.label: Day 1
strings.strategy: Add a friendly number, then take back the extra.
strings.keywords: jump, friendly number, back 1, take back.
strings.connection: First string of the routine. Sets up the open number line and jumps.
watchFor: Forgot to take back (48 on problem 3, 58 on problem 4): ask "Is 38 + 9 more or less than 38 + 10?"
Went the wrong way (49 on problem 3): ask the same question and use the line.
Counting up by ones from 38: accept the answer, then ask "Is there a faster jump?"

problems.notes: Look for: one jump of 10. Ask: "Where did you start and where did you land?"
Look for: one jump of 20, or two jumps of 10. Ask: "How is this like the last one?"
Look for: 38 + 10, then back 1. Ask: "Can 38 + 10 help you with 38 + 9?" Word choice: "jump to 48, then back 1".
Look for: 38 + 20, then back 1. Ask: "What is the same about 38 + 9 and 38 + 19?"
Look for: 38 + 30, then back 1. Ask: "Predict what someone will do."
Look for: 38 + 50, then back 1. Ask: "Before I show it, how might someone solve this?"
Look for: 38 + 100, then back 2. Ask: "How is this like problems 3 to 6? What changed?" Word choice: go over the ten (or hundred), then take back the extra.

strings.title: Give and Take
strings.label: Day 2
strings.strategy: Move an amount from one number to the other so the total stays the same and one number becomes friendly.
strings.keywords: give, take, move, same total, balance.
strings.connection: Day 1 changed one number and fixed the answer afterwards. Day 2 changes both numbers so the answer never changes.
watchFor: Both numbers moved the same way (50 + 27 for 49 + 26): ask "Did the total stay the same?"
Right amount, only one number changed (50 + 26 = 76): ask "Where did the 1 come from?"
"Add one, take one" with no reason: ask "Why does the total stay the same?" Show two jumps, one growing by 1 and one shrinking by 1.
Students who prefer Day 1's method: accept it, then ask for a second way.

problems.notes: Look for: a quick answer. Ask: "Hold on to this answer."
Look for: "same answer as problem 1", or moving 1 from 26 to 49. Ask: "What do you notice about the answer? Why?" Word choice: "give 1 to 49, take 1 from 26".
Look for: moving 2. Ask: "How many does 48 need? Where do they come from?"
Look for: 40 + 35. Ask: "Which number did you make friendly, and why?"
Look for: 60 + 35. Ask: "What changed from problem 4? What happened to the total?"
Look for: 70 + 35. Ask: "How much did you move this time?"
Look for: 200 + 45, or Day 1's way (198 + 50, then back 3). Ask: "Both work. Which is easier here, and why?"

strings.title: Subtraction as Distance
strings.label: Day 3
strings.strategy: Subtraction finds the distance between two numbers. Start at the smaller number and add up to the larger.
strings.keywords: distance, difference, gap, how far, add up.
strings.connection: The jumps from Days 1 and 2 now go from the smaller number up to the larger.
watchFor: Borrowing in their heads (21 or 12 for 100 − 89): ask "Where are 89 and 100 on the line?"
10 on problem 3: the 1 from 89 to 90 was left out. Ask "Did you start at 89 or at 90?"
24 on problem 7 (copying the pattern): ask "Are 1002 and 1000 the same number?"
Taking away instead of adding up: accept it, then ask "Which way was the shorter jump?"

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact. Ask: "How far is 90 from 100?"
Look for: "98 to 100 is 2" instead of taking away 98. Ask: "Is it easier to take away 98 or to see how far 98 is from 100?"
Look for: 89 to 90 (1), then 90 to 100 (10). Ask: "Where did you stop on the way?"
Look for: 76 to 80 (4), then 80 to 100 (20), or one jump from 76 to 100. Ask: "Which stops did you choose, and why?"
Look for: the same gap as problem 4. Ask: "What do you notice about the answer? Why is it the same?" Word choice: "same gap", "same distance".
Look for: the same gap again. Ask: "Predict 5000 − 4976 before I show it."
Look for: the gap from problem 6, plus 2. Ask: "What changed from problem 6? What happened to the answer?" Word choice: "the top number moved up 2, so the gap grew by 2".

strings.title: Constant Difference
strings.label: Day 4
strings.strategy: Sliding both numbers the same amount in the same direction keeps the difference the same. Slide both to make the subtraction friendlier.
strings.keywords: slide, shift, same difference, constant difference.
strings.connection: Day 2 kept the total by moving the numbers in opposite directions. Day 4 keeps the difference by moving both the same way. Day 3, problems 5 and 6 are the first hint.
watchFor: Slid only one number (62 − 50 = 12 for 62 − 49): ask "Did the gap stay the same?" Show both ends moving on the line.
Slid in opposite directions (63 − 48): that is Day 2's move. Ask "Did the difference stay the same?"
"Add 1 to both" with no reason: ask "What happens to the distance between two points if both slide the same way?"
Slid one number, then fixed the answer (62 − 50 = 12, then add 1): this works. Name it as another way.

problems.notes: Look for: a known fact.
Look for: the gap is still 4. Ask: "Is this harder than 12 − 8? Why not?"
Look for: 49 to 50 (1), then 50 to 62 (12), or sliding both up 1 to 63 − 50. Ask: "What did you do to make 49 friendlier?"
Look for: the same answer as problem 3. Ask: "What changed from problem 3? What happened to the answer? Why?" Word choice: "I slid both numbers up 1, so the difference stayed the same".
Look for: sliding both up 1 to 163 − 150. Ask: "Predict before I show it."
Look for: the same slide. Ask: "Does the answer depend on how big the numbers are, or how far apart they are?"
Look for: sliding both up 2 to 73 − 40, or adding up 38 to 40 to 71 (2 + 31). Ask: "Can you slide and add up? Which was quicker?"

strings.title: Choosing a Strategy
strings.label: Day 5
strings.strategy: Choose between adding up (distance) and sliding both numbers (same difference), based on the numbers.
strings.keywords: add up, slide, friendly number, efficient, choose.
strings.connection: Combines Days 3 and 4. The question is no longer how, but which.
watchFor: The same strategy for every problem: ask "Could you do it another way? Would it be quicker?"
Mixing up the slide with Day 2's opposite move: ask "Did the difference stay the same?"
Cannot say why they chose: ask "What did you notice about the numbers first?"

problems.notes: Look for: adding up. Ask: "Which strategy did you choose?"
Look for: adding up from 48, or sliding to 54 − 50.
Look for: 38 to 40 to 70 (2 + 30), or sliding to 72 − 40. Ask: "Which did you choose?"
Look for: sliding to 85 − 40, or adding up 39 to 40 to 84 (1 + 44).
Look for: sliding both up 3 to 606 − 300. Ask: "What made this one easy to slide?"
Look for: adding up 385 to 400 to 1000 (15 + 600), or sliding up 15 to 1015 − 400. Ask: "Why might adding up feel easier here?"
Look for: sliding both up 2 to 2402 − 2000. Ask: "Which strategy fits this one? How can you tell from the numbers?"

strings.wrapUp: Ask "What do you look at in the numbers to choose?" Land: if one number is close to a friendly number, add up or slide, and pick whichever you can do fastest.
